say: The sky is blue. Sunsets are orange. Same sun, same air. So what is going on up there?
Sunlight isn't really white. It's every rainbow color mixed together, and each color is a wave. Red waves are long, blue ones are short.
Air is packed with nitrogen and oxygen molecules, way smaller than a light wave. And they love bouncing short waves around.
Short waves get scattered about ten times more than red. So blue ping pongs all over the sky, and hits your eyes from everywhere.
Violet is even shorter, so why no purple sky? The sun sends less violet, and our eyes prefer blue.
At sunset, light comes in sideways and crosses way more air. Most of the blue gets bounced away before it reaches you.
What's left? Reds, oranges and yellows. A sunset is basically the sky's leftovers.
It's called Rayleigh scattering, after Lord Rayleigh, back in the eighteen seventies. Clouds? Big droplets scatter every color equally, so they look white.
And on Mars, it's flipped. NASA's Curiosity rover photographed a blue sunset, because fine Martian dust lets blue light through near the sun.
